title: The Resolute Will
author: Zhanran (annotated)
excerpt: (Excerpted from the Dream Wanderings Collection: “Instructions to the Secretary Zhihai’an”)

inline.s: (Excerpted from the Dream Wanderings Collection: “Instructions to the Secretary Zhihai’an”)

In ordinary life the old man has observed that your nature is straightforward and upright, and that you have forgotten scheming and drawn near to the Way. But your habitual tendencies are deep and heavy, and you cannot control yourself; time and again you are painfully dragged by old habits. Once you fall into the snare of Mara, your whole body sinks and falls, yet you do not know it. When suddenly you recollect yourself, you resent that you cannot leap out of birth and death, and hurriedly bestir yourself to cultivate. But when the conditions of the Way have not yet gathered and the familiar scenes of attachment appear before you, the habitual tendencies break out again, and without realizing it you drift with the waves. And by the time you turn back to look after yourself, a long while has already passed.

The old man (a self-reference of Great Master Hanshan) observes that in daily life your nature is straightforward and upright, that you have set aside scheming and drawn near to the Way. But your habitual tendencies are deep and heavy, and you cannot hold yourself together; time and again you are dragged by old habits. Once you fall into the snare of Mara, your whole body sinks and falls, yet you suffer from not knowing it in time. Only when you abruptly realize that you have again fallen into the snare of Mara do you wish you could at once leap out of birth and death, and so you hurriedly rouse your spirit to cultivate. But when the conditions of the Buddha-Way have not yet gathered and the familiar objects of emotional attachment appear before you, the habitual tendencies break forth once more, and without realizing it you drift with the waves. And by the time you turn back to take charge of yourself, much time has passed.
[Juchang] (jūcháng) means ordinarily, in daily life. [Wangji] (wàngjī) means forgetting the worldly, calculating mind, being indifferent to fame and gain, and contending with nothing in the world.
[Juan (
juàn
)] is a net for catching birds and beasts.
[Dadie] (dǎdiē) means to bestir oneself. [Daoyuan] (dàoyuán) means the conditions of the Buddha-Way.

Thus, rising and falling, you have leaned upon the old man for twenty years, and yet in the end your own great matter of birth and death has no destination whatever. Why is this? It is because you have the capacity to enter the Way, but not a will that is firm, unyielding, and decisive. Therefore you cannot stand firmly upon your heels; within your breast many evil thoughts and evil habits arise, and you are unwilling to lay a cruel hand upon them and wash them thoroughly away. To study the Way while indulging your feelings like this, not only will you not accomplish it in this life, but even across a thousand lives and a myriad kalpas you will never accomplish it.

Rising and falling like this, you have leaned upon the old man for twenty years, and yet the great matter of your own birth and death has remained without any destination. What is the reason for this? It is all because, though you have the capacity to enter the Way, you lack a will that is firm, unyielding, and decisive. Therefore you cannot stand firm upon your heels; within your breast many evil thoughts and evil habits arise, and you are unwilling to lay a cruel hand upon them and wash them clean! To study the Way while letting yourself go like this, not only will you fail to accomplish it in this life, but even across a thousand lives and a myriad kalpas, there will never be a time of accomplishment.

The Buddha said: “Difficult to hear is the Buddha-Dharma, and difficult to meet is a good friend.” Now you have been so fortunate as to meet a good friend and hear the true Dharma. If you let it slip past you face to face, when you next emerge into the world, who knows how long from now that will be? To seek even today’s circumstances then would not be possible. In this life you have been so fortunate as to meet the old man, yet your movements and stillness have never been constant. Only in the two years you have now accompanied me am I glad that you have been able to endure hardship, and one may call this a firm will. Now you take your leave again; I fear that after you leave the old man, you may not be as you are today.

The Buddha said: “Difficult to hear is the Buddha-Dharma, and difficult to meet is a good spiritual friend.” In this life you have been so fortunate as to meet a good spiritual friend and hear the true Dharma. If you let it slip past you face to face, then when you again obtain a human body (emerge once more into the world), who knows in which kalpa and year that will be? Even if you again obtain a human body, to have the opportunity of today would be impossible. In this life you have been so fortunate as to meet the old man, yet you yourself are always inconstant in movement and stillness. Only in the two years you have now spent with me am I glad to see that you are able to endure hardship and cultivate diligently; one may call this a firm will. Now you take your leave again; I fear that after you leave the old man, you may not be able to keep today’s firmness of will and endurance of hardship in diligent cultivation.

Alas, I am old now; to seek to attend upon the old man again as you do today would also be impossible. If you go through life without accomplishment, would you not be betraying this life’s one great matter and its causal conditions? Now that you are going, my earnest injunction is this: never again fall into the snare of Mara; you must hold fast to an independent integrity, and must not dwell long in the royal city.

Alas, I am old now; for you to attend upon the old man as you do today would no longer be possible. If you go through life without accomplishment, would you not be betraying this life’s one great matter and its causal conditions? Now that you are going, my earnest injunction is this: never again fall into the snare of Mara; you must hold fast to an independent integrity (you must not be dragged by emotional attachments and drift with the waves), and you must not dwell long in the bustling capital.
[Wangcheng] (wángchéng) means the capital. [
Tecao] (tècāo) means independent integrity, that is, an integrity in which one is master of oneself.

If, with the mind that has endured hardship for these two years, you serve the Sixth Patriarch as you would serve the old man, and believe in the words “this very mind is the Buddha” as you believe in the old man; if you endure your former habitual tendencies and keep them from breaking forth, rubbing and polishing mind after mind, examining and reflecting thought after thought; if you single-mindedly hold up the one topic, clench your teeth, and do not let it go readily; then, giving up this whole life to it, with an unaltering resolve: in this way, not only will you not be a single step away from the old man, but you will be in the company of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and in sitting, lying, and walking you will never step outside the practice-ground. Not only will you not betray the old man, but you will not betray yourself.

If, with the mind that has endured hardship for these two years, you uphold the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch as you would uphold the old man’s own spoken instructions, and believe in the words “this very mind is the Buddha” as you believe in the old man; if you endure your former habitual tendencies and keep them from breaking forth, rubbing and polishing mind after mind, examining and reflecting thought after thought; if you single-mindedly hold up the one topic of the huatou, clench your teeth, and do not readily let the false thoughts go; then, giving up this whole life to it, you will cultivate diligently and with an unaltering resolve. In this way, not only will you not be a single step away from the old man, but you will be in the company of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and in sitting, lying, and walking in meditation you will never step outside the practice-ground. Cultivating in this way with an unaltering resolve, not only will you not have failed the old man, but you will not have failed yourself.
[Ban] (
pān
) means to give up. For example, banming (bànmìng, to stake one’s life, that is, to risk one’s very life).
